summary: For reference-conditioned automatic mixing, prefer systems that express the result through editable conventional console controls rather than an opaque end-to-end render.
when_to_apply: When a reference song is used to guide mix style or production attributes.
what_to_change: Predict or optimize explicit gain, EQ, dynamics, pan/stereo and reverb parameters and expose them for post-hoc adjustment.
verification: Compare against an opaque baseline with level-matched listening plus several independent style/quality descriptors; inspect whether proposed control values remain plausible and editable.
cancel_if: Reject if the reference match improves only a single metric, introduces artifacts, or forces implausible/extreme controls.
source_titles: Diff2Mix: Controllable Music Mixing via Diffusion Models and Differentiable Audio Effects
evidence_note: Diff2Mix (submitted 2026-08-05) combines reference-audio style control with a differentiable console; Diff-MST is already registered in the project source registry.

summary: Do not accept an automatic/reference-guided mix because one objective score improves; evaluate several production dimensions plus listening.
when_to_apply: When ranking or accepting AI-generated mix candidates or reference-matching candidates.
what_to_change: Use a panel of independent descriptors such as spectral/style distance, RMS or loudness, stereo width/imbalance and learned distribution metrics, then require level-matched perceptual validation.
verification: Require no severe regression on protected axes and a listening win over baseline/reference-matched alternatives.
cancel_if: Do not promote a candidate when the improvement is isolated to one metric or listening reveals pumping, harshness, collapse, masking or artifacts.
source_titles: Diff2Mix: Controllable Music Mixing via Diffusion Models and Differentiable Audio Effects
evidence_note: Diff2Mix reports both objective and subjective evaluation; its listening study is limited in scale, so no universal quality claim is inferred.

summary: Test sequential stem blending as an alternative to processing all tracks independently in one pass: each new stem is conditioned on the current growing submix.
when_to_apply: Offline research when the system must handle varying numbers of stems and make context-dependent blend decisions.
what_to_change: Add stems one at a time into a growing submix and condition each decision on the current submix state; compare multiple stem orders.
verification: A/B against parallel one-pass and conventional rule-based baselines across different track counts and stem orders.
cancel_if: Reject if results are strongly order-dependent, accumulate artifacts, or underperform the parallel baseline.
source_titles: Rethinking Automatic Music Mixing as Sequential Stem Blending
evidence_note: Research preprint submitted 2026-08-06; promising paradigm, not yet a production rule.

summary: For live multitrack automation with acoustic bleed and hard latency constraints, keep a zero-latency gain-only controller as a bounded baseline before adding more complex processing.
when_to_apply: Live research/HIL tests where co-located sources bleed into microphones and audio-video synchronization makes look-ahead undesirable.
what_to_change: Predict bounded mono channel gains only, with no look-ahead, and use this as a control baseline for more advanced systems.
verification: Compare against static/manual gains on bleed-heavy live captures; measure stability, balance error and audible pumping while confirming no added algorithmic look-ahead.
cancel_if: Do not generalize this baseline to studio tone-shaping or claim EQ/dynamics quality that the cited model does not predict.
source_titles: AILive Mixer: A Deep Learning based Zero Latency Automatic Music Mixer for Live Music Performances
evidence_note: Accepted to ICASSP 2026; the published model currently predicts mono gains and explicitly targets bleed plus zero-latency live constraints.

summary: When reverse-engineering or optimizing a mix graph, fit an over-complete processor graph first, then iteratively remove negligible processors and re-optimize instead of assuming every available processor is necessary.
when_to_apply: Offline analysis/training when a target mix and corresponding dry sources are available and a differentiable processor graph can be optimized.
what_to_change: Fit the full candidate graph, rank/remove processors with negligible contribution (dry/wet can be used as a pruning cue), then fine-tune remaining controls.
verification: Compare full and pruned graphs with audio-domain loss and blinded listening; accept pruning only when perceptual quality is preserved.
cancel_if: Keep a processor if removing it causes a material audible or target-loss regression.
source_titles: Reverse Engineering of Music Mixing Graphs With Differentiable Processors and Iterative Pruning
evidence_note: JAES 73(6), June 2025. Authors report preserving full-console quality while pruning roughly two-thirds of processors; treat the exact ratio as study-specific.

summary: On well-played live rock drums, treat bleed cleanup as selective control rather than total isolation; preserve ghost notes, soft articulations and intended decay, and create aggression downstream if needed.
when_to_apply: Dense modern rock/metal drum recordings with strong performance but significant microphone spill.
what_to_change: Use gate/suppression/manual fades only as much as needed; retain live core tracks, shape tails when necessary, then add density/ambience with buses or parallel compression rather than deleting performance detail.
verification: Solo-check missed articulations, then judge all cleanup in the full mix; compare against bypass and verify that perceived size/punch improves without unnatural holes.
cancel_if: Back off cleanup if ghost notes disappear, attacks become inconsistent, cymbal tails chatter, or the kit stops breathing.
source_titles: Mixing Mike Mangini’s Drums With Dan Malsch
evidence_note: Derived from the 2026-07-27 Produce Like A Pro companion article, not from a retrieved YouTube transcript. The article reports selective spill control, preservation of soft articulations, heavy parallel compression for size, and mix-context evaluation.

summary: For a dense rock vocal, use reverb pre-delay as a candidate to keep the dry vocal perceptually forward while placing the reverb behind it; do not treat one pre-delay value as universal.
when_to_apply: When the vocal needs audible ambience but must remain intelligible and forward against dense guitars/drums.
what_to_change: Increase pre-delay while holding reverb level approximately constant, then re-balance send/return in context. Around 80 ms is a style-specific starting candidate reported in the source, not a preset.
verification: Level-match and A/B shorter vs longer pre-delay in the chorus; check that the vocal stays forward without an audible detached echo.
cancel_if: Reduce or abandon pre-delay if the reverb separates into an obvious echo, conflicts rhythmically, or makes the vocal feel smaller/thinner.
source_titles: Mixing Rock Vocals In The Box, Darrell Thorp Style
evidence_note: Derived from the 2026-04-20 Produce Like A Pro companion article, which reports a plate with about 80 ms pre-delay. Video transcript was not retrieved in this run.
